'''vagabondry†''' (vag′a̤-bon-dri), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''vagabundrye''; < ''vagabond'' + ''-ry''.] Vagabondage.

{{smaller block|Idlenes and ''Vagabundrye'' is the mother and roote of all theftes, robberyes, and all evill actes and other mischiefs.
{{right|''Laws of Edw. VI.'' (1547), quoted in Ribton-Turner’s [Vagrants and Vagrancy, p. 89.}}}}

'''vagabone,''' ''n.'' and ''v.'' A corruption of ''vagabond.''

'''Vagabundæ''' (vag-a̤-bun′dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., fem. pl. of L. ''vagabundus'', wandering: see ''vagabond''.] A division of true spiders, consisting of those dipneumonous forms which are not sedentary. They spin no web, and do not lie in wait for their prey, but prowl in search of it.

'''vagal''' (vā′ga̤l), ''a.'' [< ''vag''(''us'') + ''-al''.] Of or pertaining to the vagus, or par vagum; pneumogastric. See ''vagus''.

'''vagancy†''' (vā′gan-si), ''n.'' [< ''vagan''(''t'') + ''-cy''.] '''1.''' Vagrancy; wandering.

{{smaller block|<poem>''Springlove.'' Here are the Keys of all my Charge, Sir.
My humble suit is that you will be pleas’d
To let me walk upon my known occasions this Sommer.
''Lawyer.'' Fie! Canst not yet leave off those ''Vagancies?''</poem>
{{right|''Brome'', Jovial Crew, v.}}}}
'''2.''' Extravagance.

{{smaller block|Our happiness may orbe itselfe into a thousand ''vagancies'' of glory and delight. ''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 1.}}

'''vagans''' (vā′ganz), ''n.'' In ''music'', same as ''quintus''.

'''vagant†''' (vā′ga̤nt), ''a.'' [< ME. ''vagaunt'', < OF. (and F.) ''vagant'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''vagante'', < L. ''va-''

¶
'''vagi''', ''n.'' Plural of ''vagus''.

'''vagient†''' (vā′ji-ẹnt), ''a.'' [< L. ''vagien(t-)s'', ppr. of ''vagire'', cry, squall, bleat.] Crying like a child. ''Dr. H. More'', Psychathanasia, III. iv. 42.

'''vagina''' (vạ̄-jī′nä), ''n.''; pl. ''vaginæ'' (-nē). [= F. ''vagin'', < NL. ''vagina'', < L. ''vagina'', a sheath, covering, sheath of a scabbard, ear of grain, etc., hull, husk, vagina.] '''1.''' In ''bot.'', the sheath formed by the basal part of certain leaves where they embrace the stem; a sheath.—'''2.''' In ''anat.'' and ''zoöl.'', a sheath; a sheathing or covering part or organ; a case: specifically applied to various structures. {{smaller|(''a'') The sexual passage of the female from the vulva to the uterus. In all the higher ''Mammalia'' it is the terminal section of a Müllerian duct or oviduct united with its fellow; in the lower it is double, wholly or in part, there being two more or less complete vaginæ, right and left. In some oviparous animals, as birds, the termination of the oviduct, beyond the uterine part, receives the name of ''vagina''. See ''uterus'', and cut under ''peritoneum''. (''b'') In ''entom.'', a sheath-like plate or part inclosing an organ. In some cases also called ''valve''. Specifically—(1) The long channeled labrum of the mosquito and other blood-sucking flies, in which the lancet-like mandibles and maxillæ are concealed. (2) The jointed sheath of the promuscis of hemipterous insects, homologous with the labium of a typical insect. (3) The parts supporting and covering the tongue of a bee, corresponding to the mentum, maxillæ, and palpi. (4) The tubular sheath of the sting of a bee or wasp. (''c'') In ''Protozoa'', the indurated lorica of some infusorians, as the vaginicolous vorticellids. (''d'') In ''Vermes'', a terminal section of the oviduct, differentiated into a special canal. See cuts under ''Rhabdocœla'', ''Trematoda'', and ''Cestoidea''.}}

'''vagabond''' (vag′a̤-bond), ''a.'' an E. also ''vagabunde'', ''vacabonde'' ''vagabunde'', < OF. ''vagabond'', ''bond'' = Pr. ''vagabon'' = Sp. Pg ''vagabondo'', ''vagabundo'' = G. ''va'' ''bond'' = Sw. Dan. ''vagabond'', nomadic.
{{smaller block|Owre men suppose them to bee a ''vagabunde'' and wanderinge nacion lyke vnto the Scythians, withowte houses or certeyne dwellinge places.
{{right|''Peter Martyr'' (tr. in Eden’s First Books on America, ed. [Arber, p. 97).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death,
''Vagabond'' exile, . . . I would not buy
Their mercy at the price of one fair word.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 3. 89.}}}}
'''2.''' Floating about without any certain direction; driven to and fro.
{{smaller block|Like to a ''vagabond'' flag upon the stream.
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., i. 4. 45.}}}}
'''3.''' Of or pertaining to a vagabond or worthless stroller; vagrant.—'''4.''' Not sedentary, as a spider; belonging to the ''Vagabundæ''.

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One who is without a settled home; one who goes from place to place; a wanderer; a vagrant: not necessarily in a bad sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>Reduc’d, like Hannibal, to seek relief
From court to court, and wander up and down,
A ''vagabond'' in Afric. ''Addison'', Cato, ii. 4.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|He who goes from country to country, guided by the blind impulse of curiosity, is only a ''vagabond''.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, vii.}}}}
'''2.''' An idle, worthless stroller from place to place without fixed habitation or visible means of earning an honest livelihood; in ''law'', an idle, worthless vagrant. See ''vagrant''.
{{smaller block|Wee haue had amongst vs ''Vagabonds'', which call themselues Egyptians, the dregs of mankinde.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 590.}}}} 3. An idle, worthless fellow; a scamp; a rascal. [Colloq.]—'''4.''' One of the ''Vagabundæ''.—'''5.''' A pyralid moth, ''Crambus vulgivagellus''. See cut under ''Crambidæ''.—'''Rogues and vagabonds.''' {{smaller|See ''rogue''.}}

'''vagabond''' (vag′a̤-bond), ''v. i.'' [< ''vagabond'', ''n.''] To wander about in an idle manner; play the vagabond: sometimes with an indefinite ''it''.
{{smaller block|''Vagabonding'' in those untrodden places, they were guided by the everlasting justice, using themselves to be punishers of their faults. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iv.}}}}

'''vagabondage''' (vag′a̤-bon-dāj), ''n.'' [< ''vagabond'' + ''-age''.] The state, condition, or habits of a vagabond; idle wandering, with or without fraudulent intent: as, to live in ''vagabondage''.
{{smaller block|It reëstablished the severest penalties on ''vagabondage'', even to death without benefit of clergy. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Study of Sociol., p. 103.}}}}

'''vagabondise''', ''v. i.'' See ''vagabondize''.

'''vagabondish''' (vag′a̤-bon-dish), ''a.'' [< ''vagabond'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Like a vagabond; wandering.

'''vagabondism''' (vag′a̤-bon-dizm), ''n.'' [< ''vagabond'' + ''-ism''.] The ways or habits of a vagabond; vagabondage.
{{smaller block|As encouraging ''vagabondism'' and barbarism. {{right|''The Century'', XXX. 813.}}}}

'''vagabondize''' (vag′a̤-bon-dīz), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''vagabondized'', ppr. ''vagabondizing''. [< ''vagabond'' + ''-ize''.] To wander like a vagabond; play the vagabond: sometimes with an indefinite ''it''. Also spelled ''vagabondise''.
{{smaller block|''Vagabondizing it'' all over Holland. {{right|''C. Reade'', Cloister and Hearth, liii. (''Davies''.)}}}}

'''vagant†''' (vā′ga̤nt), ''a.'' [< ME. ''vagaunt'', < OF. (and F.) ''vagant'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''vagante'', < L. ''va''{{smaller block|{{right|''Wyclif'', Gen. iv. 14.}}}}

'''vagarian''' (vạ̄-gā′ri-ạn), ''n.'' [< ''vagary'' + ''-an.''] One given to vagaries; a “crank.” [Colloq. or rare.]

'''vagarious''' (vạ̄-gā′ri-us), ''a.'' [< ''vagary'' + ''-ous.''] Having vagaries; whimsical; capricious; irregular. ''De Morgan'', Budget of Paradoxes, p. 153.

'''vagarish''' (vạ̄-gā′rish), ''a.'' [< ''vagar-y'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Wandering; given to vagaries.
{{smaller block|His eyes were oft ''vagarish.''
{{right|''Wolcot'' (Peter Pindar), p. 305. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''vagarity''' (vạ̄-gar′ị-ti), ''n.'' [< ''vagar-y'' + ''-ity.''] The character or state of being vagarious; capriciousness; irregularity.
{{smaller block|Instances of ''vagarity'' are noticeable with each Prince of Wales, many of whom seem to have ignored, or rather not enjoyed, the title [Duke of Cornwall], although probably they did the revenues.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., II. 89.}}}}

'''vagary†''' (vạ̄-gā′ri), ''v. i.'' [Early mod. E. ''vagarie;'' appar. < L. ''vagari'' (> It. ''vagare'' = Sp. ''vagar'' = Pg. ''vaguear'' = F. ''vaguer''), wander, < ''vagus'', wandering: see ''vague'', ''a.'', and ''vague'', ''v.'' Cf. ''vagary'', ''n.'' The L. (or perhaps the It.) inf. appears to have been adopted as a whole, and accommodated to E. nouns in ''-ary;'' but this can hardly be explained except as an orig. university use. There is no L. or ML. adj. *''vagarius'' or noun *''vagaria.''] To gad; range.
{{smaller block|''Vaguer'', to wander, ''vagarie'', stray, gad, roame, raunge, flit, remoue often from place to place.
{{right|''Cotgrave.''}}}}

'''vagary''' (vā-gā′ri), ''n.''; pl. ''vagaries'' (-riz). [Early mod. E. also ''vagarie'', ''vagare'', corruptly ''fagary'', ''figary''; appar. < ''vagary'', ''v.''] '''1†.''' A wandering or strolling.
{{smaller block|The people called Phœnices gave themselves to long ''vagaries'', and continual viages by sea.
{{right|''Barnaby Rich'', tr. of Herodotus.}}
<poem>I laid the weight
Of mine Estate in Stewardship upon thee;
Which kept thee in that year, after so many
Sommer ''vagaries'' thou hadst made before.</poem>
{{right|''Brome'', Jovial Crew, i.}}}}
'''2.''' A wandering of the thoughts; a wild freak; a whim; a whimsical purpose.
{{smaller block|She’s gone; and now, sir Hugh, let me tell you you have not dealt well with me, to put this ''fagary'' into her foolish fancy.
{{right|''Brome'', Sparagus Garden, ii. 2.}}
<poem>They changed their minds,
Flew off, and into strange ''vagaries'' fell.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 614.}}}}

'''vagas''', ''n.'' Same as ''vakass''.

'''vagation†''' (vā-gā′sho̤n), ''n.'' [< L. ''vagatio(n-)'', a wandering, < ''vagari'', pp. ''vagatus'', wander: see ''vagant''.] A wandering; a roving about.
{{smaller block|Whene the mynde es stablede sadely with-owttene changynge and ''vagacyone'' in Godd.
{{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 14.}}}}

'''Vagatores''' (vag-ạ-tō′rēz), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < L. ''vagari'', pp. ''vagatus'', wander: see ''vagant''.] In ''ornith.'', a group of birds, constituting the fourth order in Macgillivray’s classification, and consisting of the crows and their allies. {{smaller|The word has no standing in science, as it designates an artificial group recognized by no other authors of note.}}
